signals.title: Introducing eve 1.0
signals.excerpt:
Published: November 17, 2026 | Authors: Andrew Barba, Shar Dara, Casey Gowrie, Colton Padden, Rui Conti, Ben Pankow, Owen Kephart, Murat Sutunc, Chad Hietala | Category: Company News

---

Today we're announcing eve 1.0, the open-source framework for building production-ready agents.

Since the public preview in June, we've worked with early adopters to prepare eve for 1.0, shipping 230+ releases and merging thousands of pull requests. With this release, eve is now generally available.

We've made eve faster, expanded integrations, and improved observability. Security controls let you decide which actions need approval and what data gets collected. We've also made it easier for coding agents to build with, measuring that experience with a rigorous evaluation suite.

With eve handling your harness and infrastructure, you and your agent can focus on building instead.

## Build production agents on a harness you own

The harness in eve is the loop that calls models, runs tools, and delegates work to subagents. You choose the model, add or replace tools, edit instructions, and decide which actions need approval. The open-source Workflow SDK saves progress as the agent runs, so it can pick up from its last completed step after a crash. Multiplayer sessions and agent-to-agent calls are built in.

For managed hosting, deploy your eve agent to Vercel. Vercel Workflows handles durable execution, and Vercel Sandbox runs agent-generated code in isolation.

Build software factories that turn requests into tested pull requests, company brains that answer questions from your business data, or customer-facing agents in your product.

...

## Give agents memory across sessions

We added native memory so agents can carry context from one session to the next. You choose the memory's scope and can use the built-in file memory, a memory provider, or one you build yourself.

Built-in `fileMemory` keeps data in memory in `eve dev` and in a private Vercel Blob store you configure on Vercel.

Other providers include claude-mem, Hindsight, Kybernesis Arcana, Memanto, memco, Supermemory, and Upstash AgentKit.

## Comprehensive AI performance across all MLPerf training benchmarks

The simplest way to read this round is per benchmark: How much more performance does the new platform deliver per GPU on the same model?

| Model type | Benchmark | GPU Count | Vera Rubin NVL72 vs. optimized GB300 NVL72 | Submission ID (Vera Rubin / GB300) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Mixture-of-Experts | DeepSeek-V3 671B | 1,024 | 2x | 6.1-0116 / 6.1-0030 |
| Mixture-of-Experts | Qwen3.5 397B GRPO (RL) | 64 | 1.4x | 6.1-0135 / 6.1-0020 |
| Mixture-of-Experts | gpt-oss 20B | 64 | 1.6x | 6.1-0135 / 6.1-0049 |
| Dense | Llama 2 70B LoRA | 72 | 1.5x | 6.1-0123 / 6.1-0138 |
| Dense | Llama 3.1 8B | 72 | 1.6x | 6.1-0073 / 6.1-0138 |
| Diffusion | FLUX.1 | 72 | 1.5x | 6.1-0124 / 6.1-0138 |
| Recommender | DLRMv4 | 128 | 1.4x | 6.1-0129 / 6.1-0038 |

Table 1. Performance per GPU of Vera Rubin NVL72 relative to GB300 NVL72, MLPerf Training v6.1, closed division

...

## DeepSeek-V3 671B: 2x per GPU on the hardest workload

DeepSeek-V3 671B is a 671-billion-parameter token-dropless Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model and the most demanding workload in the suite. Expert parallelism turns every iteration into a burst of all-to-all communication, so fabric efficiency shows up directly in time to train.

Vera Rubin NVL72 trained the benchmark in 4.14 minutes using 1,024 GPUs across 16 racks. GB300 NVL72 ran the identical 1,024-GPU configuration in 8.03 minutes, close to 2x per GPU, and the largest generational improvement in this round. Halving time to train roughly doubles how many experiments a team can run in a quarter, and experiment throughput is what moves model quality. 

At a larger scale, GB300 NVL72 produced the fastest absolute result of the round: 1.38 minutes across 10,240 GPUs. That is one training job spread across 160 racks, each its own NVLink domain, and it shows the platform’s scale-out fabric holding up long after the job outgrows a single rack.

## Post-training arrives, and Vera Rubin leads it

MLPerf Training v6.1 adds its first agentic LLM reinforcement learning post-training benchmark, Qwen 3.5 397B GRPO, reflecting a fundamental shift in AI development. Post-training has emerged as the critical differentiator for agentic accuracy, making the GRPO workload uniquely demanding. The continuous cycle of generating rollouts, scoring them, and updating weights pushes system architectures to their limits by forcing constant, massive weight migrations between inference and training engines.

Vera Rubin NVL72 achieved the fastest time for this new benchmark with a time of 10.44 minutes at 1,024 GPUs (6.1-0117), compared with 13.78 minutes for GB300 NVL72 (6.1-0031) at the same scale. The Vera Rubin platform also proved its flexibility by submitting on two different inference backends: NVIDIA NeMo RL with TensorRT-LLM at 10.44 minutes and with vLLM at 10.94 minutes (6.1-0118). Shipping two viable inference backends on a benchmark this new says as much about software maturity as it does about silicon.

Teaching these models to observe, reason, and act requires running each rollout in a simulated environment and executing tool calls, code, or API validations. Because driving these simulations is intensely CPU-bound, the NVIDIA Vera CPU is integral to the architecture, sustaining more than 22,500 concurrent RL environments across 256 CPUs in a single Vera CPU rack. 

While the GPUs handle massive token generation and rapid weight updates, the Vera CPUs work in lockstep to simulate the environments, ensuring the accelerators are continuously fed with the rich feedback required to perfect agentic workflows.

signals.title: Persistent Sessions and Memory for Strands with MongoDB | MongoDB
signals.excerpt:
November 18, 2026 ・ 5 min read

Today, we’re launching the MongoDB Strands Harness SDK Integration, available now as the open-source strands-mongodb Python package. Strands, built and maintained by AWS, is an open-source framework for building AI agents. With this integration, MongoDB becomes the single data platform behind your Strands agents, providing:

- Session persistence, so agents can resume conversations and complex tasks after a restart or on a different instance.
- Long-term memory for facts and lessons that carry across conversations.
- Vector search to retrieve relevant past interactions by meaning.

Strands’ MemoryManager decides what to remember and when to recall it, while MongoDB handles where it’s stored and how it’s retrieved, so there’s no custom memory code to build or maintain. And because your operational data already lives in MongoDB, agents can use Atlas Vector Search to ground their answers in it, with no copy synced to a separate vector database.

## What is the Strands Harness SDK?

The Strands Harness SDK helps developers build AI agents. It manages the agent loop while giving developers control over how agents execute tasks and maintain context. Support for memory, sessions, and hooks lets developers shape agent behavior and connect agents to their application’s data and persistence layer. It provides pluggable storage and memory interfaces, with built-in backends for local files and Amazon S3. Integrations like this one let you swap in another backing service without rewriting your agent’s core logic.

...

## What does the MongoDB Strands Harness SDK Integration provide?

This integration covers three core areas:

- Cross-environment continuity: When a different instance handles the next request, or a user returns after a restart, the agent retrieves its saved session from MongoDB. Continuity doesn't depend on any machine.

- Resilience to failure: If a host crashes or a container is rescheduled, another instance resumes the session from the last turn written to MongoDB.

- Retention and control: You decide how long sessions and memories are retained, with separate retention periods for each. A memory store can also delete a single memory, or all of its memories, on demand. Everything lives alongside your application's operational data in MongoDB, under the access controls and backups you already have in place. 

The memory store also handles what production agents run into:

- No duplicate memories: Strands can extract the same fact more than once. A content hash turns the repeat into a no-op.

...

- Tenant scope: The store stamps every memory with a scope, such as a tenant or user ID, and limits every search and delete to that scope. Callers can't override it through filters or metadata. This isolation is enforced by the package, not by the server, so where a tenant boundary is also a compliance boundary, give each tenant its own database or collection, with credentials restricted to it, and MongoDB enforces the boundary itself.
- Search adapts to your deployment: The integration supports Vector Search, Text Search via Atlas Search, or Hybrid Search combined with $rankFusion. The store automatically selects the optimal method available in your deployment, and each result indicates which search type was used.
- OpenTelemetry tracing. Every operation records a span on the tracer your application already uses, and no memory content is captured.

...

Memory, with no embedding pipeline to run: Atlas Automated Embedding embeds each memory for you, using voyage-4-lite unless you choose a different model. You write plain text and search with plain text. There's no embedding library to install and no model API key to manage. Atlas generates, stores, and updates the embeddings itself as memories are written, so there's no batch job to keep vectors in step with the text.

...

signals.title: Cerebras Launches Disaggregated Inference
signals.excerpt:
Nov 17 2026

# Cerebras launches disaggregated inference

We’ve deployed Cerebras Wafer Scale Engines with GPUs to deliver lightning-fast tokens at scale

The world is hungry for ultrafast tokens. In 2026, Cerebras saw an insatiable demand for fast inference, both on our inference cloud and via our partners. To meet demand, we began developing disaggregated inference: GPUs handle prompt processing (prefill) and Cerebras systems handle output generation (decode).

This solution is now in production and delivers five times more tokens per megawatt at the same ultrafast Cerebras speeds.

We can now serve more ultrafast tokens via Cerebras Inference Cloud to meet market demand. Infrastructure partners can also leverage the Cerebras disaggregated solution to achieve more ultrafast tokens in their own datacenters.

Alongside our recently announced CS-4, our dramatically scaled manufacturing, and our planned 700MW of data center capacity, disaggregated inference will enable Cerebras and partners to serve many more ultrafast tokens in 2027 and beyond.

...

### Why Cerebras is advantaged for decode

An inference request has two main stages. Prompt processing, known as prefill, processes the input and produces intermediate model state. Response generation, known as decode, uses that state to generate output tokens. There are many ways to split the inference workload, including draft–target and attention–FFN among others, but separating prefill from decode is uniquely advantageous when the goal is highly interactive inference.

Decode is autoregressive. That means the model generates one token at a time, using each generated token as an input to generate the next. Each step means reading model data from memory again, so memory bandwidth matters a lot. In the ultrafast inference domain, SRAM-centric chips have an advantage because they can keep that data on-chip and read it much more quickly. Cerebras takes this to wafer scale, with tens of gigabytes of SRAM and tens of petabytes per second of memory bandwidth on a single chip—350× the SRAM capacity and 5,400× the memory bandwidth of a typical GB300 GPU. This allows the Cerebras System to fit more concurrent requests and model layers directly on the chip, enabling the CS-3, CS-4, and CS-5 to achieve ultrafast speeds at an attractive throughput.

### Cerebras disaggregated inference production results

Pairing Cerebras systems, which are optimized for ultrafast decode, with accelerators well-suited to the compute needs of prefill, such as AMD Instinct GPUs, allows the delivery of an immense amount of ultrafast inference at scale. In a production deployment on the Cerebras Inference Cloud, AMD Instinct GPUs process prompts, and Cerebras CS-3 systems generate responses. Moving prompt processing to GPUs allows Cerebras systems to devote their serving capacity to response generation. In our measured production deployment, this combination delivered 5X the throughput per megawatt of a CS-3-only configuration, with no loss in token generation speed.

Source: November 14th shared GPT-OSS-120B endpoint via the Cerebras Inference Cloud throughput per megawatt before and after enabling disaggregated inference, normalized to the aggregated inference baseline (1×). 

We plan to deploy disaggregated inference broadly across hundreds of megawatts in the Cerebras Inference Cloud and in partner deployments by the end of 2027. Our aim is to increase the ultrafast inference capacity available for our customers.

### Cerebras disaggregated inference for infrastructure partners

The Cerebras disaggregated inference solution was also built for our partners to adopt. Infrastructure partners can deploy disaggregated inference clusters based on Cerebras-provided reference architecture, co-locating their chosen prefill accelerators and Cerebras systems within a unified network. For software integration, partners can either integrate with the Cerebras end-to-end disaggregated software stack or a decode-only SDK.

The end-to-end disaggregated software stack is best suited for partners optimizing time-to-market. It consists of:

- A disaggregated inference framework to route requests between prefill and decode pools and manage replica capacity and health.
- A prefill engine to process prompts using open-source inference engines like vLLM or SGLang.
- A Cerebras decode engine for response generation on Cerebras systems.
- KV Portal software, an interface to transfer intermediate model state, including key-value caches, between prefill and decode engines over RDMA.

The decode-only SDK is best suited for partners optimizing for control. With the decode-only SDK, partners can bring their own inference framework and prefill engine to the Cerebras decode engine and KV Portal software. In addition, the decode-only SDK provides development aids such as a mock Cerebras decode replica and a reference integration to an open-source disaggregated inference framework and prefill engine.

signals.title: The evolution of GraphRAG: Advancing systems and evaluation together - Microsoft Research
signals.excerpt:
### At a glance

- GraphRAG Zero gives AI agents the connected context they need to reason, make decisions, and act, built and updated continuously at interactive speed. 
- It’s the result of years of research, turning graph-based retrieval from an experimental technique into a deployable system built for real-world applications and agents.
- GraphRAG is now available as an option in Foundry IQ (Azure AI Search), so customers and developers can use graph-guided retrieval at scale.
- Knowledge graphs are built on Microsoft Research’s GraphRAG research, bringing commercial, graph-guided retrieval to Foundry IQ (opens in new tab) and GitHub’s Repo Mind Light, supporting applications from scientific discovery to repository understanding.
- From dataset-wide sensemaking to interactive retrieval, GraphRAG’s evolution has reduced cost and latency while preserving access to relevant, representative evidence.
- The original paper now has 3.9k citations since April 2024 and the open-source repo (opens in new tab) has over 36k GitHub stars. It has spawned a wide range of follow-on research and software.

GraphRAG Zero is designed to solve one of the fundamental challenges preventing AI agents from reaching their full potential — giving them the context they need to reason, make decisions, and act intelligently. 

AI agents need more than text excerpts that merely match the words in a prompt. To answer complex queries and understand connections across different kinds of information, they need retrieval that captures the structure within the data. This becomes increasingly important as AI generates more information than people can review. GraphRAG provides that structure, while its latest version, GraphRAG Zero, makes retrieval fast and affordable enough to build and update continuously.

...

When we shared our GraphRAG research and open-source library (opens in new tab) in 2024, we introduced a way to ask questions that conventional retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) struggled to answer. Instead of finding only individual facts or passages, people could ask about themes, patterns, and implications across an entire collection of documents.

The impact extended beyond adoption of our library. GraphRAG helped broaden the field’s focus from finding relevant passages to organizing connected evidence for reasoning across a dataset. Today, new research approaches and open-source implementations explore this design space, while industry tooling makes graph-based retrieval available to application developers.

...

The result has been two connected lines of research: successive generations of GraphRAG, and an evolving evaluation framework, BenchmarkQED (opens in new tab). Together, they have now brought a new and lightweight version of GraphRAG – GraphRAG Zero – into products. Compared to the original GraphRAG, this version eliminates LLM calls at index time and can be configured to retrieve relevant context without LLM calls at query time either, delivering sub-second retrieval latency powered entirely by the geometry of text embeddings.

GraphRAG Zero is now available as an option within Foundry IQ (Azure AI Search) (opens in new tab), bringing graph-guided retrieval to applications that need relevant, representative evidence at interactive speeds. Microsoft Discovery is also committing to adopt GraphRAG Zero through Foundry IQ to support scientific research. 

GitHub Next’s Repo Mind Light (opens in new tab), a tool for repository understanding, ships with GraphRAG Zero and is available as a public container integrated with GitHub Agentic Workflows (opens in new tab). It combines GraphRAG Zero retrieval over issues and pull requests with live retrieval of code and documentation, giving people and coding agents context for questions about architecture, ownership, and the reasoning behind earlier decisions.

...

LazyGraphRAG reduced preparation costs by moving language-model work to query time. The resulting delay before answer generation, however, remained a constraint for interactive applications. GraphRAG Zero addresses this with an embedding-derived graph that assembles relevant, representative context. In its real-time configuration, generative-model processing is reserved for the final response. The research evaluation below helps explain the approach behind today’s release; these results are not measurements of the Foundry IQ service.

...

In the GraphRAG Zero study, we applied these measures to podcast transcripts and news articles using 200 synthetic questions, split equally between multi-hop and global queries. At a 50-chunk retrieval budget, global answer assertion coverage increased from 53.4 percent with vector RAG to 57.4 percent with GraphRAG Zero. Both used the same embedding model and answer generator, producing one response per query. GraphRAG Zero prepared the answer context in 0.93 seconds on average, including query embedding and excluding answer generation.

Sub-second retrieval changes the experience of asking a question. LazyGraphRAG and deep-research-style workflows can spend a minute or more gathering and analyzing evidence; here, answer generation can begin almost immediately. That is the practical meaning of “Zero”: retrieval at the pace of an interactive conversation.

GraphRAG Zero achieved higher cluster recall and topical fidelity, while vector RAG retained higher chunk precision. More representative evidence supported more complete global answers, showing why the relevant-chunk fraction alone was insufficient to guide development.

signals.title: Hugging Face describes CQ quantization and GCMP adapters · Tensor Journal
signals.excerpt:
Published Nov 16, 2026 2 min read

Tensor Journal

## Key facts

Organization

Hugging Face

Other

Nov 14, 2026

huggingface.co

Hugging Face says it describes CQ, a calibration-free quantization format, and GCMP, a parameter-efficient adapter positioned as a replacement for LoRA. The material is dated November 14, 2026.

Hugging Face says CQ needs no calibration data. Its input is a Hugging Face checkpoint, and it runs layer by layer. The post says GCMP is compatible with CQ, NF4 and full-precision bases.

Hugging Face lists the CQ model at 18 GB and the NF4 model at 22.4 GB.

The benchmark model is Qwen3.8-27B. In company-reported results, the CQ base scores 0.65 on GSM8K. Hugging Face says CQ shows no significant difference from BF16 across all benchmarks. It reports an NF4 loss of 12.0 points on GSM8K against BF16. Hugging Face gives the benchmark size as 200–1,140 questions per task.

The post reports mean KL divergence on WikiText-2 of 0.0282 for CQ against BF16, and 0.033 for NF4 against BF16.

On Qwen3.8-27B, GCMP has 2.9M parameters, and its adapter is about 11 MB on disk. LoRA at rank thirty-two has about 159M trainable parameters and occupies about 320 MB on disk.

The adapter runs used the Alpaca dataset and a fixed set of training settings, covering steps, batch size, sequence length, learning rate and random seed. Hugging Face says those settings were identical across the compared runs.

Hugging Face reports that, on an NF4 base, GCMP scored 4.0 points higher on GSM8K (p = 0.04) than LoRA.

On ARC-Challenge, Hugging Face reports that CQ with GCMP was lower on ARC-Challenge (−4.2, p = 0.001) than NF4 with GCMP.

Hugging Face says the CQ + LoRA run is still in progress. The first CQ + LoRA adapter it evaluated came from an older trainer version, which the post describes as broken.

Hugging Face reports that CQ trainer step time fell from 27.6 seconds per step before a recent improvement to 8.6 seconds now.

Hugging Face says vLLM serving of GCMP currently requires a CQ base, while GCMP adapters on full-precision models run in Transformers for now. CQ supports pipeline parallelism across GPUs, but tensor parallelism is not yet supported. The post gives a per-token adapter routing buffer in vLLM of ~1 MB.

The CUDA kernels ship compiled. Hugging Face says they include a license check and are free during early access.

signals.title: DaisyRose-27B: Pushing the Frontier of Post-Training Efficiency | RadixArk Blog
signals.excerpt:
November 18, 2026

# DaisyRose-27B: Pushing the Frontier of Post-Training Efficiency

Today we are releasing DaisyRose-27B, RadixArk’s first model, built on Qwen3.8-27B and trained with reinforcement learning using Miles. We trained it on long-horizon agent tasks with sessions up to 1M tokens, with just 1,200 curated tasks in 18 days on 144 H200 GPUs. DaisyRose-27B improves Terminal-Bench 4.1 pass@1 from 5.6% to 12.0%. Beyond Terminal-Bench 4.1, it also delivers gains on a variety of other reasoning, instruction following, and coding benchmarks.

We are releasing BF16, FP8, and NVFP4 checkpoints for everyone to try and build on. In this post, we explain how carefully designed tasks and efficient infrastructure made these gains possible on a limited compute budget.

DaisyRose-27B scores higher than the original Qwen3.8-27B model on every benchmark above 1. The largest gain is on Terminal Bench 4.1, a notoriously hard long-horizon benchmark. Our magic lies in the following three key ingredients: high-quality training data, efficient training backend, and robust sandboxes.

...

We built the tasks in partnership with Eigent AI, starting from Eigent AI’s large pool of tasks in machine learning, software engineering, science, and other fields. Together we built thousands of candidates.

...

- Each task targets a mistake the original model makes.

...

Each attempt gets up to 1.5 hours in the sandbox, with more than 100

...

## Efficient training backend

RadixArk trained DaisyRose-27B with Miles, our open-source reinforcement learning framework for large-scale model post-training, in fully asynchronous mode: the agent keeps working while the model learns, and neither waits for the other. While 128 H200s run the inference on agent tasks, 16 more run the trainer and learn from the trajectories. After every step, the updated model goes out to the 128 GPUs that run the agent. The learning runs on our internal training backend, which is built for agent training: each step learns from a handful of very long sessions, some as long as 1M tokens, folded into multiple trajectories via harness summarization.

57% lower training cost. On this release, 37% of each GPU's peak compute went into useful training work (model FLOPs utilization, or MFU) on our backend. The open-source trainer, built on Megatron, reached 16% on comparable runs. So the same training needs 57% less GPU time. The gain is even larger on mixture-of-experts models: 6.2× on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, and more than 10× on the roughly 300B-parameter GLM-5.3-Flash.

2× faster end to end. Counting the time the agent spends on its tasks, the release run trained on about 16,800 tokens per second across its 144 GPUs. The open-source trainer reached about 8,300 on the same GPUs.

Stable over weeks. The release run trained for weeks on 144 H200s, 63,000 GPU-hours in total. From the first step to the last, its speed and efficiency held steady.

...

## Robust sandbox service

During training, every attempt the agent makes runs in a sandbox: a fresh copy of the task's environment where the agent runs commands, edits files, and is then graded. All of the RadixArk team's work on this release ran in sandboxes on our own service, built on the open-source AgentENV project, to which we also contribute fixes. Between mid-September and mid-November, the service ran about 944,000 sandboxes for this project, with up to 1,566 running at the same time.

Reliable as it grew. The service grew from a single machine to as many as 12. We shipped ten upgrades to it, nearly all of them while training was running. Across all nine weeks, 99% of sandbox creations succeeded, and since late October more than 99.95% have. Getting there took a steady stream of fixes and improvements, such as keeping a machine from freezing when it runs out of memory.

80% lower cost. Our cloud infrastructure cost for the project's sandboxes was about 80% lower than the cost of running the same sandboxes with popular cloud sandbox providers. One way we keep costs down is to give each sandbox memory that grows and shrinks with what it actually uses. A sandbox usually uses only a small part of the memory it asks for, so each machine can run many more sandboxes.

signals.title: SenseNova Loop-9B Official Release: Deeper Computation with
signals.excerpt:
2026/11/17 47 Share

SenseTime has officially released SenseNova Loop-9B. Building on the Preview version’s exploration of parameter efficiency, the model reuses layer parameters through a Loop structure and incorporates manifold-constrained hyper-connections (mHC) to extend computational depth with approximately 9B parameters, supporting complex reasoning, coding, tool use and multimodal tasks. Thanks to its efficient looping architecture, the official 4-bit quantized weights occupy only about 4.9GB, with deployment GPU memory requirements as low as under 10GB. This significantly broadens the range of compatible hardware, making it possible for chips with limited GPU memory to deliver performance comparable to leading 27B-class models.

Since the Preview release, we have received considerable community interest and feedback on model usage, inference deployment and ecosystem integration. The official release retains the Loop and dual-stream mHC architecture, further improves performance on agent, coding and data analysis tasks, and continues to explore how looped computation can enhance model capabilities.

SenseNova Loop-9B has approximately 9B parameters in total. By executing shared intermediate layers twice, it expands 32 physical decoder layers into 56 layer computations. The model accepts text and image inputs, produces text outputs, and supports a context length of up to 512K tokens. In agent and data analysis evaluations, it demonstrates competitiveness comparable to Qwen3.8-27B: its NL2Repo score of 41.36 approaches Qwen3.8-27B’s 44.60, while its AIDABench score of 65.31 exceeds the latter’s 65.01.

Model Highlights

- Shared loop module: Layers 4–27 form a weight-sharing loop module that runs twice, enabling 56 decoder-layer computations in a single forward pass.
- Dual-stream mHC: Learnable mappings route and fuse information across two residual streams within the loop module.
- Hybrid attention: The decoder uses groups of four layers, combining three linear-attention layers with one full-attention layer.
- Long-context multimodality: The training regimen covers text, images, code and tool-use trajectories, extending context length to up to 512K tokens.
- Resource-efficient on-premises deployment: With 4-bit weight quantization and an 8-bit KV cache, inference at a 256K context length requires approximately 15 GiB of GPU memory, lowering the barrier to local and on-premises deployment.
- Official quantization available on day zero: An official AWQ 4-bit quantized version is available from launch day for rapid deployment.

SenseNova Loop-9B model weights and related code are now available for developers and researchers to download, deploy and explore.

...

Deployment on Hardware with Limited GPU Memory

Thanks to its looped weight-sharing structure, the model requires only approximately 9B distinct parameters, with 4-bit quantized weights occupying about 4.9GB. This substantially lowers hardware requirements for local and on-premises deployment. An 8-bit or 4-bit KV cache can further reduce GPU memory requirements for long-context inference. The table below shows minimum deployment memory requirements at different KV quantization precisions:

Current Limitations and Ongoing Improvements

Although the Loop Transformer architecture has demonstrated considerable potential, model size and development time mean that SenseNova Loop-9B still has room for improvement in the following areas:

- With numerous or complex tool definitions, or multiple conditional constraints, the model may still make interpretation and execution errors that affect task performance.
- Coding capabilities have improved substantially over Preview and are now practical for many uses. However, consistency on coding and general-purpose agent tasks remains an area for improvement, although the model can correct its mistakes through additional steps. Overall, its ability to handle complex, long-horizon tasks requires further refinement.

signals.title: Microsoft Retriever 1: Sub-Second Agentic Retrieval in Foundry IQ
signals.excerpt:
MattGotteiner

Nov 17, 2026

By: the Foundry IQ microsoft-retriever-1 team Today, we’re introducing Microsoft Retriever 1 an agentic search model trained by Microsoft and available in Foundry IQ. It’s available in preview today, with no provisioning or reindexing.

#### Key Points

- microsoft-retriever-1 is an agentic search model trained by Microsoft and hosted entirely within Azure's security envelope.
- Agents that delegate retrieval to microsoft-retriever-1 use a third fewer input tokens, with the highest cited recall and answer correctness.
- microsoft-retriever-1 requires no provisioning or re-indexing. Enable it on Foundry IQ search queries or on a knowledge base.
- Adding microsoft-retriever-1 to auto retrieval reasoning effort in knowledge bases cuts typical latency by more than 6x.
- Adding microsoft-retriever-1 to Foundry IQ search queries improves evidence recall by 8-11 points.

# Fully managed agentic retrieval in Foundry IQ

In most agentic RAG systems, one large language model manages interactions with the user and drives the retrieval system. It infers information needs, writes search queries, and decides to search again or produce an answer. Every turn of that loop adds a network round trip and fills the context window. Changing models requires tuning the prompts driving the entire system.

With the introduction of Microsoft Retriever 1, Foundry IQ allows you to offload agentic retrieval tasks to an Azure-hosted model. Microsoft Retriever 1 interprets the underlying information need from user queries, reformulates those queries using terminology from documents in your corpus, and returns more relevant results. Enabling Microsoft Retriever 1 in your existing Foundry IQ solution requires no additional provisioning or document ingestion.

In Foundry IQ knowledge bases, auto retrieval reasoning effort replaces the agentic retrieval loop with Microsoft Retriever 1, escalating to a larger language model only when required. After an initial search, Microsoft Retriever 1 reviews the results and decides whether to search again. In our evaluations, only the hardest 20% of queries escalated to that larger model. Compared with a knowledge base using medium retrieval reasoning effort with gpt-6.1-sol, pairing microsoft-retriever-1 with gpt-6.1-sol cut typical latency nearly 6x and gpt-6.1-sol token usage by more than 75%, while retaining 90% of its evidence recall.

...

## Experiment 3: Agents that delegate retrieval to Microsoft Retriever 1 use 32% fewer input tokens and get more answers right

Every agent needs relevant context. To understand how agents might use agentic retrieval to find that context, we provided gpt-6.1-sol with access to search tools powered by BM25, BM25 with semantic ranking, and BM25 with microsoft-retriever-1. We first required gpt-6.1-sol to use each tool, then let it choose among all three on its own. The system prompt described the technology behind each tool. We then ran our full private and public datasets through each configuration.

| Method | Cited recall | Answer correct | gpt-6.1-sol input tokens | Mean turns | Mean citations |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| BM25 | 68.5% | 63.3% | 9,595 | 1.6 | 5.3 |
| BM25 + semantic ranking | 72.9% | 66.6% | 7,960 (-17%) | 1.5 | 4.6 |
| BM25 + microsoft-retriever-1 | 74.8% | 69.1% | 6,465 (-32%) | 1.4 | 6.0 |
| gpt-6.1-sol choice | 73.0% | 67.6% | 7,960 (-3%) | 1.5 | 5.6 |

Cited recall is evidence recall computed only from the documents gpt-6.1-sol cites in its answer.

Requiring gpt-6.1-sol to delegate all retrieval to microsoft-retriever-1 reduced input token usage by 32% compared with BM25 and 19% compared with BM25 + semantic ranking, while also delivering the highest cited recall and answer correctness. It also beat letting gpt-6.1-sol choose its own search tool. gpt-6.1-sol picked simpler retrieval approaches 75% of the time, which required follow-up turns.

signals.title: Introducing Amazon OpenSearch Memory: Persistent memory for AI agents | AWS Big Data Blog
signals.excerpt:
Today, we are announcing the general availability of Amazon OpenSearch Memory, a new capability built on Amazon OpenSearch Serverless for adding persistent memory to AI agents. OpenSearch Memory stores agent interactions as searchable events, derives useful memories, and retrieves relevant context across sessions. You can give agents long-term memory without provisioning infrastructure or building separate extraction, indexing, consolidation, and retrieval systems.

AI agents need memory when an interaction depends on information from an earlier session. A support agent might recall a customer’s open case and product configuration, a coding agent needs repository conventions and prior decisions, and a personal assistant keeps a user’s preferences. An agent that restarts or hands off a conversation also needs the exact turns that came before. Passing the complete conversation history to the model becomes slower and more expensive as that history grows, and the relevant information can be difficult to find.

Building a memory system requires more than storing transcripts. You must capture events, extract facts and summaries, generate embeddings, reconcile new information with existing memories, retrieve the right context, isolate data, and enforce retention and deletion policies. You must also operate the infrastructure and evaluate whether the retrieved memories improve agent responses.

OpenSearch Memory manages these functions as one serverless capability. Your application writes conversation events after each turn and searches for relevant memories and events before generating a response. OpenSearch Memory stores the original events verbatim, makes them searchable within seconds, and asynchronously derives structured memories. It handles extraction, embedding, indexing, consolidation, retrieval, data isolation, and retention.

...

The write and retrieval paths operate independently:

1. After each interaction, your application writes the conversation turn to a space as an event. OpenSearch Memory stores the event verbatim (`CreateEvent`) and indexes it for keyword, semantic, and hybrid search. Events are available to read immediately and become searchable within seconds.
2. In the background, the memory strategies configured on the space extract memories from these events.
3. OpenSearch Memory compares each new memory with the existing ones and adds, updates, or skips it, so stored memories stay current.
4. Before the agent responds, your application retrieves context: memories about the user from past conversations, the exact turns of the current or earlier conversations, or both. Your application adds the retrieved context to the model’s prompt.

signals.excerpt:
Nvidia uploaded Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-NVFP4-QAD on Nov 17, 2026—a 180B image-text MoE with aggressive ModelOpt QAD mixing NVFP4 and MXFP8. How it differs from NVFP4.

Nov 17, 2026· 8 min read· Yash Thakker

NVIDIA on November 17, 2026 added a second public quantization experiment atop Qwen3.8-Flash-Next: `nvidia/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-NVFP4-QAD`, an image-text-to-text mixture-of-experts checkpoint exported with ModelOpt QAD after 100 optimizer updates. It ships the full multimodal stack— vision encoder, PLE n-gram embedding, and MTP module—in roughly 129.7 GB of safetensors shards.

For local inference engineers, the important distinction is naming: -QAD means quantization-aware training tweaks, not merely re-labeled NVFP4 weights. NVIDIA''s card warns the recipe is more aggressive than `Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-NVFP4` and that accuracy gains are not statistically established.

## TL;DR

| Item | Model card claim |
| --- | --- |
| Base model | Qwen/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next |
| Training stack | NVIDIA ModelOpt + NeMo AutoModel (FSDP2) |
| QAD steps | 100 optimizer updates |
| Expert precision | NVFP4 routed + shared experts (trained) |
| Extra layers | GDN / QSA / indexer projections → MXFP8 |
| Disk footprint | ~129.7 GB weights |
| HF task | image-text-to-text |

## What QAD changes in the weight stack

A model core split into matching shards for distribution, echoing consolidated NVFP4 and MXFP8 safetensors

The Hugging Face README includes a component table. Summarized:

- Main LM routed experts (48 MoE groups) stay NVFP4 block size 16, trained with QAD.
- Shared experts (144 linear matrices) move to NVFP4 under QAD—where the earlier NVFP4-only release left them differently.
- GDN projections (180 matrices) use MXFP8 blocks under QAD.

NVIDIA explicitly says the repository name''s -QAD suffix identifies the method, not a promise that the old NVFP4 recipe stayed intact.

Consolidation note: NVIDIA merged shards for distribution, verified SHA256 against export, and claims tensor names, shapes, dtypes, and values are unchanged—relevant if you diff against internal checkpoints.

November 16, 2026

Tencent today announced the release of Hy4 flash, the latest addition to its Hy model family. Hy4 flash has 224 billion total parameters (including 64 billion Engram parameters) with only 12 billion active parameters, and supports multimodal inputs and a context length of up to 1M tokens. It is the most cost-effective Hy model to date, priced at approximately US$0.070 per million input tokens, US$0.281 per million output tokens, and US$0.003 per million cached input tokens — a substantial reduction from Hy4.

Hy4 flash vs Hy4 API Price Comparison in USD (https://hy.tencent.ai/research/hy4-flash)

To achieve this level of cost performance while maintaining strong intelligence and practical utility, the Tencent Hy team made a series of engineering choices across the model pipeline:

- Pre-training: Hy4 flash incorporates hybrid attention, LatentMoE, and Engram architectural features. The KV cache size is just 1/24 that of Hy3 and 1/6 that of Hy4. Extensive scaling ladder experiments were conducted to ensure performance met expectations.
- Post-training: Drawing directly from Hy4’s architecture, the model inherits strong general intelligence. Reinforcement learning cuts average end-to-end task output tokens by 50 percent.
- Evaluation: The team built WorkIndex, an internal benchmark based on typical WorkBuddy tasks, paired with human evaluations, focusing on deliverable quality, single-turn output length, and task turnaround time rather than public benchmark scores detached from everyday work.
- Inference: Combining optimization using megakernel, 4-bit quantization, and DFly techniques, Hy4 flash achieves decoding speeds exceeding 150 tokens per second, enabling low-cost deployment at scale.

As a result, Hy4 flash slightly outperforms the larger Hy4 Preview (770 billion total parameters, 49 billion active parameters) in overall effectiveness, at a significantly lower cost. Based on the internal WorkIndex benchmark, which covers PowerPoint deck creation and editing, document editing, spreadsheet repair, audio/video processing, and visual understanding tasks typical of use with WorkBuddy — Hy4 flash delivers a per-task cost of just 1/13 that of Hy4 Preview, 1/20 that of Hy4, and 1/8 that of DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 (Max tier, peak-hour pricing).

signals.title: Co-Designing Sparse Attention for Efficient Long-Context Inference | NVIDIA Technical Blog
signals.excerpt:
Nov 17, 2026

...

Agentic workloads, long documents, and large codebases are pushing context lengths from tens of thousands of tokens to hundreds of thousands. At those lengths, attention becomes the most expensive part of a transformer layer. Dense attention scores every query against every key, so its cost per query grows with the context length N, and at 128K tokens it can take most of the prefill time in a layer.

The model-level solution is sparse attention, a transformer technique in which each query attends to only a small subset of the context, chosen per query, instead of all of it. This cuts both the compute and the memory traffic of attention on long context.

This post is a practical primer for model developers designing sparse attention that runs well on NVIDIA GPUs. It focuses on model-level sparse attention, where sparsity is trained into the model, rather than drop-in methods applied after training such as BLASST, MInference, or Quest. A production FP8 kernel is used to sweep the indexer’s design knobs (query heads, key heads, head dimension, compression ratio, and speculative-decoding depth), measure how Top-k cost scales, and compare token-level with block-level core attention.

Each section explains what the hardware rewards and why, and ends with a guideline you can apply to your own design. This post follows the same co-design approach as the earlier posts on dense attention and hardware-friendly LLM design.

# Buoyant launched Kinference open source inference control plane for Kubernetes

Building on top of the open source vLLM inference engine, Kinference allows organizations to provide safe, reliable, and cost-effective inference across multiple models, GPUs, and machines, while delivering the governance and policies needed for enterprise use at scale.

Kinference is lightweight, easy to deploy, and can be run without a team of specialists. It is agnostic to LLM model, cloud provider, and GPU type. Kinference’s feature set lets organizations offer a true, internal “inference platform” that provides inference guardrails and controls, lowered cost of inference, intent-based routing, burst to cloud, and per-tenant usage and cost attribution.

Kinference can be paired with an enterprise's existing stack. Like an LLM gateway, using Kinference is simply a matter of pointing inference clients to its HTTP endpoint and sending OpenAI or Anthropic-compatible inference traffic there. The goal, according to Buoyant, is to enable every organization in the world to own their own intelligence with a secure, reliable, internal inference platform.

In public Kinference benchmarks, when compared to standard Kubernetes load balancing, Kinference decreased median time-to-first-token (TTFT) by 95% and median end-to-end latency by 45% of requests on one workload type.

Kinference is fully open source under Apache v2. It’s available on GitHub.

By Sergey Kostenchuk Published 2026-11-16 Updated 2026-11-18

...

Baseten published the basetenlabs/deepseek-ultrafast repository containing a Rust and CUDA engine written for DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, targeting NVIDIA B200 and B300 GPUs with sm_100a and sm_103a architectures. According to the README, decoding reaches 2060 tokens per second on a setup of eight B300s in a TP8 configuration: one step takes 2.71 milliseconds with an average accepted block length of 5.6 tokens, while 1740 tokens per second are claimed on four GB300 accelerators. Prefilling one million tokens fits within 11.7 seconds, equivalent to 85,000 tokens per second. The engine supports a 1-million-token context and can share the KV-cache across multiple servers via Redis and RDMA. According to the authors, GPU kernels were refined by coding agents working with FlashInfer and SGLang sources, and the DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-Fast model is delivered to clients via Baseten Model APIs through the OpenAI-compatible endpoint inference.baseten.co.

...

### What is currently unknown / limitations

All key figures are taken from Baseten's own README and refer to the batch=1 mode after warm-up: there are no independent public replications or detailed measurement methodologies yet, so the metrics should be treated as a hypothesis subject to verification. Due to speculative decoding, the actual speed will depend on the proportion of accepted draft tokens for a specific model and load. Direct comparison with Cerebras and Groq is incorrect: this is a measurement of single-stream latency for a single request versus metrics from specialized accelerators obtained on other models and methodologies. The engine only runs on sm_100a and sm_103a architectures, i.e., on B200, B300, and GB300, and will not work on other hardware. Finally, the thesis about recursive self-improvement remains the post author's interpretation, not an established fact: humans are still participating in the optimization loop.
